title: Punjab's shared devotional ground
hook: a queen left alone at the forest's edge, and the poet who finds her

segments.voice: Yesterday, Punjab's shared devotional ground: Vaisakhi, one spring day, the same fields, each neighbor keeping its own meaning. Did someone tell you what a day means to them? Day one thousand four hundred eleven.
screen: `THE SAME DAY, EACH ITS OWN MEANING.`

segments.voice: A woman sits alone at the edge of a forest, crying. She is Sita, the queen of Ayodhya, and she's carrying a child. Ram has sent her away because of what people in the city were saying, and the brother who drove her here has gone back. Some young students from a nearby hermitage hear her and run to tell their teacher. The teacher comes out to her. He's Valmiki, the poet of the Ramayana. And he finds the heroine of his own story weeping at his door. Today, our last day in Punjab, and a place that tradition says is that door.
screen: `SITA ALONE AT THE FOREST'S EDGE.` → `THE STUDENTS RUN FOR THEIR TEACHER.` → `VALMIKI COMES OUT.`

segments.voice: In the last book of Valmiki's Ramayana, in paraphrase, Valmiki speaks gently to Sita. He tells her he knows she has done no wrong. He brings her into his hermitage and gives her into the care of the women there, to be looked after like a daughter. Notice the shelter first. The poet who tells the whole story of Ram also becomes the one who shelters Sita when the story turns hard on her. Her twin sons are born there, Lava and Kusha, and they grow up in the hermitage. Valmiki teaches them the Ramayana, and in the story they sing it, their own father's story, before Ram himself. Then the place, in Punjab. Tradition places Valmiki's hermitage at Ram Tirath, near Amritsar. There's a temple and a sacred tank there, and pilgrims come to the place where, the story says, Sita found shelter and her sons were born. And last, who honors him. Tradition calls Valmiki the first poet, the adi kavi. In Punjab, the Valmiki community honors him with special devotion as Bhagwan Valmiki, and his birthday is kept with processions. Each comes to him in its own way, and the place holds them all. And that's where our regional journey ends: Tamil hymns, Bengal's streams, the Varkari road, Kashmir, Kerala's Onam and Ayyappa, Gujarat's courtyard of questions, and Punjab, where songs and festivals and holy places are held as shared ground. Tomorrow, before the festivals that close the year, we stop and sit at the top of the climb.
screen: `VALMIKI SHELTERS SITA` · `THE TWINS LEARN THE RAMAYANA` · `RAM TIRATH, NEAR AMRITSAR` · `HONORED BY EACH IN ITS OWN WAY`

segments.voice: Remember a shelter. Sit, and let the breath settle. Think of a time when life turned hard and someone took you in: a friend's couch, a teacher's office, a grandparent's kitchen, a kind word at the right moment. Let that person come to mind. Feel what it was like to be sheltered. Then, for a few breaths, simply wish them well. If you pray, you can hold them before God. The bell holds the time.
Punjab's shared devotional ground. Today, Ram Tirath, where tradition says Valmiki sheltered Sita and her sons learned the Ramayana. Today's word.
Your line: Punjab's shared devotional ground. Today, be a little shelter for someone having a hard day: a seat, a meal, a listening ear. Day one thousand four hundred eleven.

Confirm Uttara Kanda details: the students (muni-kumaras) tell Valmiki; he assures Sita he knows she is innocent; she is given into the care of the ascetic women; twins born there; they later sing the Ramayana. Some tellings place the twins' birth story differently (e.g. Kusha made from grass in later versions); the script keeps to twins.
'The Ramayana itself calls him that' (adi kavi): the Ramayana tradition calls Valmiki the first poet; a Keeper should confirm the phrasing or soften to 'tradition calls him the first poet'.

Confirm Ram Tirath (near Amritsar) as Valmiki's hermitage in Punjabi tradition, with a temple and sacred tank, and the Valmiki community's devotion to Bhagwan Valmiki with Valmiki Jayanti processions. A reader from the Valmiki community should check the framing.
